items.question: How do you think about the architecture that enables Exo to improve itself?
items.object: Exo's recursive self-improvement architecture
items.answer: In a nutshell, Exo is an agent that's fully recursive. It's able to safely edit all aspects of itself at runtime to get better at the task that it's working on. It's enabled by this very minimal but opinionated harness architecture that splits different pieces of what an agent is today into components that can be safely isolated from each other and thus safely evolved. We can talk much more about how it does this, but I think you should think about it as an agent that really does full recursive self-improvement.

It's enabled by this very minimal but opinionated harness architecture that splits different pieces of what an agent is today into components that can be safely isolated from each other and thus safely evolved. We can talk much more about how it does this, but you should think about it as an agent that really does full recursive self-improvement.

The response explains that isolating Exo's agent components from one another enables those components to evolve safely.

items.question: Why do you see agent harnesses as a new layer in the ML stack?
items.object: Agent harnesses as a new layer in the ML stack
items.answer: I think it's enabled today by the fact that we're entering a new layer in the ML stack, in my mind, where up until recently we've still been really focused on trying to make models better at what they do. When we say models, we're talking about the weights. You are training the model. First it was large pre-training runs. Then it became applying fine-tuning to these models to get them good at a particular task in their thinking. I think the shift over the last year to agents has made us much more aware of the power that lies in the harness, the tooling, the body that we provide to the brain of the LLM. The shift that's happening now is we're starting to realize that as we tweak these harnesses, they get really good at particular tasks, either better at doing them or more efficient, doing them with fewer token calls, less usage, driving cost down. Costs are a huge concern right now because frontier models keep getting more expensive because they're larger, harder to serve, require more GPUs, etc.

items.question: Why do you want to collapse the optimization loop into the system itself?
items.object: Collapsing the optimization loop into a self-improving system
items.answer: The project came from my spending the last year or so of my research at Berkeley on discovery systems. AI-driven discovery, right? This project came out of the SkyLab at Berkeley, called Sky Discover. It was this outer loop that tries to optimize and improve a system. What I got really curious about was: How do we take this to its extreme? You have some outer system that's optimizing some inner system. What if you want to optimize the way you're doing your optimizing? Then you need some outer outer loop, and it's this infinite recursion out. The only way I think out of that is to collapse that loop down and make it so that the system itself is responsible for improving itself, which I'm calling to collapse the loop. So it's very different than having an outer observer that's looking and trying to make changes to the other system as it's running. I want the system to be able to change itself at runtime. And this is the thesis for Exo.

items.question: How do you assess the kind of self-improvement OpenClaw makes possible?
items.object: OpenClaw's adaptability and self-improvement
items.answer: I think the thing that OpenClaw really discovered was how to make an agentic system that feels magical in that it adapts to your workflow. It is adaptable. But I want to point something out: it's adaptable in a very particular, narrow way. If we were to look at the architecture, there are particular places where the OpenClaw folks have made it extensible. The one dynamic, super-dynamic way is memory. All of these agent systems have some sort of memory. Literally, it is a memory MD file somewhere. There is a markdown file that things get written to. It gets injected in context every time the LM constructs a call, and we can edit that file. That's the main super-dynamic way. Otherwise, OpenClaw exposes places where you can extend it. You can add skills. You can ask the agent, "Here, look, go look at this skill, please add it." You can add tools. By the way, this is very often driven by a human. A human will come in and say, "Hey, I want a skill for this. Let me go install this skill," and then ask OpenClaw to do this. So it's absolutely self-improvement and extensibility. Memory is a form of self-improvement. But there's so much more going on inside these agents.

items.question: How do you conceptualize the agent policy that Exo aims to make recursively self-improving?
items.object: Agent policy and Exo's recursive self-improvement
items.answer: I think about an agent as an LM call that's wrapped in machinery that's used to construct context. It's really a big context construction machine, and it also provides a way of executing actions. Part of the context is, "Here are the things I can do," and the LM can say, "Please go execute this tool or this action," and the agent is responsible for actually taking that action and then reflecting it back. The machinery for constructing that context, all of that, I call policy. What goes into policy? It could be how you assemble the actual LLM call. Do you take the last 10 messages in your history or the last 100? That's going to be more expensive but provide more information. Or do you take the last 10 messages and then a summary of the previous 90, which is how we think about compaction? These are all policy decisions that are static, defined for OpenClaw or Pi or Claude Code if you look at their source code. That's the policy of what an agent is: the tools it can use, the skills it has, how it includes them in its context, how it constructs context, anything about the actual agent's code. That's what Exo sets out to make fully recursively self-improving. It's not just certain points where you can insert additional skills. It has changed the very machinery of what skills are for your job.

items.question: Why do you believe Exo should let an agent change its entire architecture rather than just add plugins as OpenClaw does?
items.object: Exo’s approach to making agent architecture self-improving
items.answer: I've marked here in red the parts that are plugins. There are places that make this customizable for your particular task. Let's say that you're working on something that's doing development, looking at a whole bunch of sets of different docs. You might want the docs for a bunch of different projects in your memory, but you might want to run RAG over them to fetch the most relevant ones to include in the context. This memory plugin allows you to say, "Here's a different way of storing and indexing your memories." Great. A human comes along and sets that. Or there's tools, and you can say, "Here's an additional tool I want to give to my OpenClaw," or skills. There are all the ClawHub sites that list out tools or skills that you can install. This is all still a human coming in and modifying; you can say, "Please install this tool for me." But the shift that we're trying to make is all of the other things that are not red here—all the connective arrows, all the components—we believe all of that needs to be improvable by the agent, especially as the agents keep getting better. As they keep getting better, it's this bitter lesson: you don't want to over-specialize because you don't want the human deciding all these architecture bits. As the model gets better, it knows how to architect the agent in a way that's most optimal for the given task. That's the shift. If I were to put EXO's architecture next to this, I'd put red lines around all components here and say they are all changeable by the agent itself.

items.question: Why do you see a running agent modifying itself as more powerful than a separate agent modifying it?
items.object: Runtime self-improvement in Exo compared with a separate agent modifying it
items.answer:
I'll just point out you are still trusting a machine when you have an outer separate agent modifying the inner agent. It's still not you making the changes, right? You're maybe helping direct it, but you still have to have the same trust in the machine that's making the changes. The question is, do you have an external system that inspects an internal system, or do you let the running system itself inspect itself? The cool thing when you merge the two layers together is that the same system that's deciding to make changes is also deciding what to run and what to inspect. Your system itself can try things and look at how it does and how its own internals perform, and make changes to itself as it runs.

I can give you a really good example. We've had Exo running, playing Pokémon, and while it's running, the system itself decided to try inspecting the RAM of the game. Then it mapped the RAM—people have reverse-engineered this manually in the past; they figured out what components in the memory map do different things in the game. In the memory there are certain places where you store the positions in the world, the Pokémon that's currently active, whether you're in a battle or not. Literally booleans in the code, in the memory. Exo was able to modify its own integration with the game and feed this into the system message to better inform its decision-making as it progresses. An outer loop would have to think about that and potentially try a design, tell it, launch it, see how it does, reflect back. If the system itself is evolving, as it makes changes it can inspect things and use that runtime inspection to inform its design process. So I think it's a more powerful, more fully expressive way of doing self-improvement than an outer system.

items.question: How do you see your systems background shaping your approach to AI agents?
items.object: A systems perspective on AI agents
items.answer: I'm coming strictly from systems. I started my PhD before ChatGPT really took off, and I was a core networking person. I've done my work in core systems, designing wider network architectures for SDN controllers—just how you decide what path your data takes through the internet. Then I do formal verification for networks, and I've come from a lineage of really thinking about system architectures and trade-offs and designs. I'm not an ML person coming down into agents. I'm a systems person coming up.

items.question: Why do you think agent harness architecture will remain valuable as language models improve?
items.object: Agent harness architecture as a way to enforce properties independently of model alignment
items.answer: My bet is this: people keep trying to get models to do things that align with their goals, and alignment is an unsolved problem. We keep trying to align these models to do the right thing. In harness space, we actually have an opportunity to enforce certain properties by the architecture of the system that we design, which is totally different than trying to bet on the model, the LLM, the weights containing the rules that we want. For example, if you never want to delete your history, you have to enforce that in the architecture of your harness rather than just asking in context, "Please, LLM, don't ever do anything that'll delete my history," because we keep seeing that there's ways to trick the model. So that's the place that I think architecture holds and really shines for a systems person.

items.question: Why do you favor decomposing an agent into Exo's three separate layers?
items.object: Exo's separation of agent policy, protected state, and sandbox execution
items.answer:
This project, Exo, is a self-improving agent, but that's enabled by this architecture for the harness that's opinionated and very carefully partitions agents. I just want to draw the parallel to how we think about agents today. When you think of Claude Code, Claude Code is both an agent—people colloquially think of it as an agent—and it's also a harness, and they're kind of shipped together. You drop it into an environment where it works. A common workflow for me is I spin up a VM, go in there, start Claude, and work on a project. I clone a repo. I have to log in with my GitHub credentials so it can go and push things for me, and then I'm working in this isolated space. I trust it relatively, and then I dangerously skip permissions so that in this VM—and by the way, I can accept here—oh, this is kind of risky because I've actually logged in. I have to have my keys there, maybe; I certainly have my GitHub credentials there. But okay, at least it's not going to destroy my computer because it's running in a VM somewhere.

The architecture that we're proposing decomposes the idea of an agent into three distinct important layers: an executor, an Exo harness, and a sandbox. These layers all have different properties. This is very important. We think of the Exo harness as needing to keep all state—the minimal set of things that we want to have protected from the agent. It's stuff that the agent uses, but that we want to have protected. The executive contains all of the policy. Policy entails how you assemble your context, what are your prompts, how do you do compaction, what are your skills, what are your tools, anything about how the actual agent is deciding what it's going to do. In this way we have a really nice split. The executive is fully stateless, a fully stateless process. The Exo harness contains the layer that has the conversation history, any secrets that might be needed such as API keys, artifacts or snapshots of an environment.

Finally, we have a sandbox layer, which is the actual environment where things are happening. This is not supernatural to think about because today Claude Code runs in the same environment as the code itself that it's editing. You drop it in, and Claude Code is running as a process on your machine, editing other files on your machine. Or you drop Claude Code into a VM, where it runs in a VM and is editing files on that VM. We split that out, where the actual actions—the agent wants to run a bash command of some sort—get executed in a sandbox distinct from the actual policy process that can be running anywhere else. What this gives you is a nice split: it gives you an isolated execution environment, protected state, and a very explicit stateless layer that's safe for self-evolution. The executive can propose changes to itself in a way that you will not lose any history. You won't leak secrets because they're not exposed to the LM itself. Our Exo harness provides a mechanism for snapshots. This is really nice because you can snapshot the sandbox environment, and the agent—the policy itself—can choose at runtime as it's running to try to make some changes and roll itself back.

This is the fundamental architecture behind Exo. An agent now—and this is the hardest piece, I think, in understanding Exo and the Exo harness architecture—is decomposed, split across these three layers. It is the conversation history that's stored in the Exo harness, the state plus the policy that's running, which is an executive, plus a sandbox that it's running on. Those together define an agent as we think about them today.

items.question: What do you see as the minimal architecture that allows Exo to be a fully recursive, self-improving agent?
items.object: The architecture enabling Exo to be a self-improving agent
items.answer:
In my view, you have sandboxes, you have a harness that holds on to your state that's fully stateful, and you have the executive. You have policies: all the compaction, tools, skills, LM call, etc. The step that Exo takes, what really makes EXO a self-improving agent, is it will mount in its sandbox its own code for the executive itself. As a result, the part of the decision-making that the LM can make is it can say, "Hey, go edit some aspect of its own harness at runtime." We have in the Exo harness a special guardian process that will allow the executive to be rebuilt at runtime, mid-step, and also provides some sort of soaking process where, after being rebuilt, we try to bring up the executive, let it proceed one step, and if it breaks itself off accidentally, it'll get rolled back to the previous state automatically.

Those are the minimal set of components that are needed, because now you have an executor that can see its own code. It can edit its own code. It can ask to rebuild its own code and swap mid-run, and as a result—and finally—it's protected by an Exo harness that will roll it back. This mechanism can build new tools, write new skills, change anything about how the context is assembled, adjust adapters, etc. So that is the final step that allows EXO to be fully recursive.

items.question: Where do you see the real benefit of teleporting agent state and sandbox environments in the Exo harness architecture?
items.object: Teleportation of agent state and sandbox environments in the Exo harness architecture
items.answer:
In a world where you're running a single agent working on a single task, there is very little need for teleporting your stuff away. You either run it locally while you're working, or if you want it to just be always on, you have to run it remote to begin with. It has to be on a server somewhere so that when you shut your laptop, it's still going. The benefit here is, what if you want to scale up to working on a bunch of different tasks in parallel? You have a bunch of different conversations. This is a very real need. It's not a need for you and me managing our email, but it could be a need for a company.

Let's say a company is wanting to spin up a conversation in an agent, or a dedicated agent, to each user's usage logs. The user comes in, uses your app, you have some library that logs to a database. There's a stream of events coming in, and there's some kind of reasoning you want an agent to do over that stream as it happens. You might want to wake up a dedicated sandbox environment for each of those conversations, which is fully doable in the Exo harness architecture. If you're trying to do this for 100 users, great. It's going to fit on your one machine, up to 100 containers running at once. If you want to do this for 50,000 users, you're going to start running out of space on your machine. You might have enough policy processes because you only need a couple to be awake at a time, but you're going to have a lot of different customers being woken up at different times and different dedicated sandboxes coming up. A benefit of teleportation is once you start running out of space for running sandbox containers on your machine, you can start moving some of them off to the cloud—either starting new ones up in Daytona or moving existing ones up to Daytona or some other provider. You might want to give access to resources that aren't available locally. That's the benefit I see of teleportation.

items.question: How do you think about the division of responsibilities between the executive and the Exo harness?
items.object: The division between executive code and runtime state in the Exo harness
items.answer:
When subagents run, what tools do they have, what access do they have—all of that, to me, is up in the executive and is used at runtime. The simple Exo as it's built today doesn't natively come with subagents, but it absolutely can be implemented in the same pattern, just in code. The way to think about this executive is it's a block of code, and these modules here are really me laying out conceptually what components go in that block of code. It's up to you how you write that code.

State that you have, for example, like memory: you might see memory here. The way you choose to record or inject memory lives in the executive, but the actual memories themselves go down in the Exo harness as artifacts for that conversation or for that agent. It's kind of like how you do things is defined in the executive; the actual state at runtime lives in the Exo harness.

items.question: Why do you think the Exo harness should keep its secret store separate from the agent’s sandbox?
items.object: The secret store in the Exo harness
items.answer: The secret store is really great. We want it to live in the Exo harness so that it's not exposed directly to the LLM. If you think about dropping an LLM—let's say you're working on a project building a harness—even for that harness to be able to run in your environment, you probably need an API key. If your agent is running in the same environment as your API key, that is now fully exfiltratable, fully readable. It's very helpful and handy, and actually quite important, to separate out a secret store that stays in the Exo harness on the host process from the sandbox in which operations are taking place. That secret is kind of injected in the executive without actually exposing it in the space where the tools can see what is being used, which is in the container.

items.question: Why do you think real-time agents might need a better notion of interruptible work?
items.object: Interruptible work in real-time agents and OpenClaw's architecture
items.answer: As I think about how this needs to change, there might need to be some better notion of interruptible work for agents on their side. This is another thing that I've noticed has bothered me with the OpenClaw architecture. As wonderful as it is, once an agent starts working on a thing in a thread, that thread is not interruptible. As a thing is off working, if you try to ping it, it just won't respond. You don't even know what it's doing, which is really frustrating. So the way you have to get around this is you start a different conversation. You say, "Hey, do you know what's going on over in that other thread? Like, why is it not answering?"

items.question: How do you think agent architectures need to support interactive, interruptible work?

items.answer: We're going to need to reinvent what that interactive, interruptible work looks like in the agent layer, which is separate from the work going on in the model layer and in this interactive model space. items.question: What excites you about giving Exo access to the costs of its own conversations?
items.object: Exo's cost-aware self-improvement
items.answer:
One very standard thing that you might want your agent to do is run more cheaply. Costs for inference are really high. One of the big issues is even just how do you assemble your context? How much of the history do you include? I can tell you with OpenClaw, my bills for running OpenClaw ran way up because of the way it assembles its context. It puts so much stuff in there. One of the things we did in Exo, which is really cool—the Exo harness conversation log stores not just what you talked about, but it's also annotated with costs for each of the messages. Because of that, the executive has access to constructing context and also reasoning over the past conversations and the costs associated with different parts of those conversations.

Very early on, one of the first things that was most exciting to me was after we built self-improving Exo, we asked it—actually, I asked, "Hey, how much did the last message cost in the Discord adapter?" It was 16 cents. It's like, "Are you serious? 16 cents? That's actually crazy. Go work on driving that down." It went and rearchitected its own Discord adapter at runtime, made changes, observed them, tested them, to really scope down the context that was included in each of the LM calls as they were built, by scoping it to certain conversations and certain threads only rather than pulling messages from across different threads in Discord. That drove down the cost by, I think, like a 96% decrease. We committed this back afterwards. The changes it made improved itself, decreased cost, and then we ended up committing that to the actual code that's there now.

The problem of specifying what you want to an agent is still an open one. I expect us to build out a bit more tooling in the context, providing it that as it improves itself it should also track performance and define some way of tracking that.

items.question: Why do you think the agent harness layer makes recursive self-improvement possible now in a way it wasn't before?
items.object: Recursive self-improvement at the agent harness layer
items.answer:
I want to point out something that's happened in the last six months, which is we've moved from iterating on model weights, training model weights, to iterating on this harness and this agent layer. The big difference here is that the medium for these agents, for this harness layer, is the same as the actual building material. items.question: Why do you welcome people into the Exo community even if they only want to discuss the topics?
items.object: Participation in the early Exo community
